1.pericope_label: The burden of Moab: because in the night Ar is laid waste, every head shall be bald and every beard cut off

schools.summary: Supplies the political history from Saul and David down to the revolt after Ahab's death, and turns to the inscribed Moabite stone for what the biblical record leaves obscure, identifying the high places and reading Nebo as a city rather than the mountain.

Asks who the oracle was for and answers that it was never sent to Moab at all, so that its use is to keep believers from thinking the world governed by fortune; and denies that the first place named is a proper name.
Dates the prophecy and its fulfilment, treats this chapter and the next as one prophecy improperly divided, and gathers comparative evidence for the shaved head as a token of mourning.
Gives three reasons why an oracle against a foreign nation was preached to Judah, and reads the night attack as a warning against dwelling securely.

debates.question: Why was an oracle against Moab delivered to Judah?

positions.view: for three reasons: that judgment beginning at the house of God does not end there; as proof of God's care of his own and enmity to their enemies; and because a prophecy fulfilled within three years would confirm the prophet's mission

because it was never addressed to Moab at all, neither by voice nor in writing, so the prophet looked to believers, that seeing kingdoms overturned they might not think the world governed by the blind violence of fortune

debates.question: Does it matter that the cities fell in the night?

positions.view: yes: the inhabitants were probably given to ease and dwelt securely, and we should lie down as those who do not know what a night may bring forth
the circumstance is somewhat unusual but not material enough to be so strongly insisted on
it means only suddenly and unexpectedly

outliers.reading: Alone treats this chapter and the next as one entire prophecy very improperly divided into two, and observes that Jeremiah took much of it into his own longer oracle against the same people, so that comparing them rectifies transcribers' mistakes in both.

Alone contrasts the obscurity of Moabite history and its unidentifiable towns with the world-drama of the burden of Babylon, and repairs the deficiency from the inscribed Moabite stone found at Dibon.

themes: The burden of Moab. Because in the night Ar of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence; because in the night Kir of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence;
He is gone up to Bajith, and to Dibon, the high places, to weep: Moab shall howl over Nebo, and over Medeba: on all their heads shall be baldness, and every beard cut off.
In their streets they shall gird themselves with sackcloth: on the tops of their houses, and in their streets, every one shall howl, weeping abundantly.
And Heshbon shall cry, and Elealeh: their voice shall be heard even unto Jahaz: therefore the armed soldiers of Moab shall cry out; his life shall be grievous unto him.

5.pericope_label: My heart shall cry out for Moab: the waters of Dimon shall be full of blood, and lions upon him that escapeth

schools.summary: Keeps the pity the prophet's own, adopts the harder reading of the difficult clause about bars rather than fugitives, admits ignorance of two place names, and finds a pun by which the last of them is bent towards the word for blood.
Explains the lament as a prophetic convention rather than a private emotion, applies the heifer to the untouched town the fugitives run to, and offers alternatives for the drying of the waters.

Settles the disputed pronoun from the versions so that it is Moab's own heart that cries, supplies a naturalist's reason for choosing a heifer, and glosses the cry of destruction as the sound of men falling into the pit.
Draws the ministerial lesson that God's servants should be of a tender spirit, and turns the plundered storehouses into a warning to those eager to lay up this world's goods.

debates.question: Whose heart cries out for Moab?

positions.view: the prophet's, pitying fellow creatures though they were enemies; though others, with the Targum, refer it to the Moabites themselves
Moab's own: the Greek and the Chaldee read his heart, not mine, so render it the heart of Moab crying within her
the prophet's, touched with pity though a stranger to Moab and belonging to a hostile people
neither exactly: the prophets customarily assume the character of those whose calamities they foretell, exhibiting their condition as if upon a stage, which strikes harder than direct instruction

debates.question: What is the point of the heifer of three years old?

positions.view: its voice: in cattle alone the female's is deeper, so a heifer's lowing is the apter image for mourning, though the expression is very short and obscure
its wildness: a scare as of a heifer not yet tamed by the yoke
its security: the figure belongs to the town the fugitives run to, in full vigour, never having felt the yoke and never having been attacked
its grief: a heifer lowing for her calf

outliers.reading: Alone raises the objection that the prophet ought rather to have lamented the ruin of the Church and rejoiced at the fall of her enemies, and answers it by making the lament a convention of prophetic style.
Alone admits that neither of the two places named in the flight can be identified, offering only that one name may indicate a staircase of boards and the other two caverns.

themes: My heart shall cry out for Moab; his fugitives shall flee unto Zoar, an heifer of three years old: for by the mounting up of Luhith with weeping shall they go it up; for in the way of Horonaim they shall raise up a cry of destruction.
For the waters of Nimrim shall be desolate: for the hay is withered away, the grass faileth, there is no green thing.
Therefore the abundance they have gotten, and that which they have laid up, shall they carry away to the brook of the willows.
For the cry is gone round about the borders of Moab; the howling thereof unto Eglaim, and the howling thereof unto Beer–elim.
For the waters of Dimon shall be full of blood: for I will bring more upon Dimon, lions upon him that escapeth of Moab, and upon the remnant of the land.
